title: Chapter 115 — Hiring: Finding the Right People
intro: You can train skills. You cannot train desire. This chapter teaches you what to look for when hiring — and why attitude and ambition matter more than a resume full of product knowledge.

sections.title: The Hiring Principle
sections.content:
One principle has consistently shaped my hiring decisions across every role I have held — from sales manager to store manager to director to president of sales.

You can train skills. You cannot train desire.

I can teach product knowledge. I can teach the 10 Steps of Selling. I can teach objection handling. I can teach closing. I can teach CRM. I can teach presentation skills.

I cannot teach hunger. I cannot teach work ethic. I cannot teach competitive drive. I cannot teach passion for improvement.

Those qualities must already exist. Hiring should prioritize attitude and ambition over technical knowledge.

sections.title: What You Are Really Looking For
sections.content:
When you interview someone, you are not looking for the person who knows the most about appliances. You are looking for the person who wants it the most.

The person with twenty years of product knowledge but no drive will coast. They will hit a comfortable income level and stop improving. They will do enough to keep the job but never enough to grow it.

The person with zero product knowledge but genuine ambition will learn everything you teach them. They will ask questions. They will stay late. They will study on their own time. They will outperform the veteran within a year — not because they are smarter, but because they want it more.

I have seen this happen dozens of times. The resume does not predict success in sales. The attitude does.

sections.title: Questions That Reveal Drive
sections.content:
Standard interview questions — 'tell me about yourself,' 'what is your greatest weakness' — tell you almost nothing about whether someone will perform on a sales floor.

Better questions include:

Tell me about a time you had to teach yourself something difficult. What did you do?

What was the hardest thing you have ever worked for? How did you get it?

If you had a slow day with no customers, what would you do with your time?

How do you handle being told no?

What does success look like to you in one year?

These questions reveal work ethic, self-motivation, resilience, and ambition. Those are the qualities that predict performance on the floor. Product knowledge can be taught in weeks. Character takes a lifetime to build — and you either have it or you do not.

sections.title: The Danger of Hiring for Experience Alone
sections.content:
Experienced hires can be a gift or a liability. The gift is that they know the industry, know the products, and can start selling immediately. The liability is that they bring habits from their previous environment — and those habits may not be the ones you want.

An experienced salesperson who learned to sell at a competitor may have developed shortcuts, bad habits, or a process that conflicts with yours. They may resist coaching because they believe they already know how to sell. They may be complacent — comfortable earning a certain income and uninterested in growth.

I am not saying never hire experienced people. I am saying do not hire them just because they have experience. Evaluate the same things you would evaluate in anyone: drive, attitude, coachability, and willingness to improve.

The best experienced hires are the ones who say 'I have been doing this for ten years and I still want to get better.' Those are rare — and valuable.

sections.title: Hiring for Culture Fit
sections.content:
Every team has a culture — whether you built it intentionally or it formed on its own. A hire that does not fit the culture creates friction for everyone.

If your team is competitive, driven, and holds each other accountable — hiring someone who is passive, comfortable, and resistant to feedback will drag the culture down. Not because they are a bad person. Because they are a bad fit.

Conversely, if your team has become complacent and you are trying to raise the bar, hiring someone hungry and ambitious can disrupt the status quo in a positive way. That person becomes the example that shows what is possible.

Hiring is not just about filling a position. It is about building the team you want.

sections.title: Coaching Rule
sections.content:
When evaluating hiring decisions, ask:

Are you hiring for skills or for drive?
Does the candidate show genuine ambition — or are they just looking for a job?
Can they articulate what success looks like to them?
Are they coachable — willing to learn your process even if they have experience elsewhere?
Do they fit the culture you are building?
Would you trust them on the floor with your best customer?

You can teach someone every product in the showroom. You cannot teach them to care. Hire the ones who already care.
